newsitem.title: USA: FTC again rejects Staples merger with Office Depot.
newsitem.headline: FTC again rejects Staples merger with Office Depot.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission on Friday rejected a restructured $4 billion merger of Office Depot and Staples Inc.

The action sets the stage for the FTC to go to Federal District Court to seek a preliminary injunction that would block the merger, but a spokesman for Staples said no decision had been made whether to carry the fight that far.
"We are evaluating whether to fight this in court," said Todd Krasnow of Staples. "We have to see precisely what the FTC has said and need to take it under considerartion with the board of Staples."
In a statement, the FTC said the deal would lead to higher prices if permitted.

"FTC rejects proposed settlement in Staples/Office Depot merger, says deal would still violate antitrust laws and lead to higher prices for office supplies," the FTC said in announcing a press conference for later in the day. The commissioners' vote was not announced.
The argument that prices would increase under the deal had been made all along by the Ralph Nader Consumer Project on Technology.

"What the commission did was great," said James Love, an economist with the project. "This was an important case. The fundamental is: is two (office superstores) enough. Today the commission said no, two is not enough."
The decision leaves three players in the field. Staples and Office Depot each have around 500 stores. The third player is OfficeMax, which has between 700 and 800 stores.
The chief executives of both Staples and Office Depot expressed bitter disapppointment.
Staples CEO Thomas Stemberg said, "We do not understand their rationale." Office Depot CEO David Fuente called the decision "absurd."
Staples and Office Depot announced the proposed merger last fall, but it was delayed several times as the government sought more information about the merger.
Last month the FTC rejected the merger 4-1. After that, Staples and Office Depot changed the proposal by agreeing to sell 63 stores to OfficeMax.

Staples and Office Depot argued that their competitors extended far beyond the three chains of superstores and included everyone from the corner pharmacy selling school supplies to giant discounters selling computers, furniture and office supplies in bulk.

In addition, the firms argued that their merger would actually lower costs to consumers because of increased efficiencies. To carry their message to the public, they ran full-page advertisements quoting small merchants and others saying they felt certain the merger would lead to lower prices.

After the FTC announced its decision, Office Depot stock dropped $5.125 to $14 on the New York Stock Exchange, while Staples was up 87.5 cents at $22.125 on Nasdaq. OfficeMax was off 75 cents at $12.25 on the NYSE.
